lessons.title: Reading a Population Pyramid: Dependency Ratios and What They Signal

children.text: The last lesson gave you the stages. This one gives you the tool analysts actually use to place a country on that ladder at a glance: the population pyramid. Once you can read one fluently, you can look at a chart you have never seen before, for a country you know nothing about, and say within seconds whether its workforce is about to expand or its pension bill is about to explode.
What a Population Pyramid Actually Shows

A population pyramid stacks a country's population in 5-year age bands, from 0 to 4 at the bottom up to 80 plus at the top, with men on one side and women on the other, each bar's length showing how many people sit in that band. Nothing about the chart is exotic. It is a horizontal bar chart, twice over. What makes it powerful is what its overall shape reveals, in one image, about decades of past births and the decades of future workforce and retirement load that are already locked in.
Three broad shapes recur across countries, and each maps directly onto the stages from the last lesson.

body.text: India's national pyramid today is best described as a dome that is still filling in at the top. The base has already started narrowing, this is the falling TFR from the last lesson showing up visually, while the 20 to 40 age bands remain the widest part of the chart. That bulge is the working-age population this whole course is ultimately about.

children.text: The Dependency Ratio: Turning a Pyramid Into One Number

markDefs.definition: The population aged 15 to 64, treated by convention as the segment capable of full-time paid work. It is a statistical convention, not a claim that everyone in this band works or that no one outside it does.

children.text: A shape is useful, but analysts need a single comparable number, which is where the dependency ratio comes in. It measures how many people outside the
, conventionally those aged 15 to 64, each working-age person is effectively supporting, whether through direct family income, taxes, or public spending.

body.caption: Expressed as a percentage: every 100 working-age people are supporting this many dependents, split between the young and the old.

children.text: Splitting this into two halves matters, because a youth-heavy dependency burden and an elderly-heavy one have almost opposite economic implications. A country with a high youth dependency ratio is spending heavily on schools today in exchange for a workforce tomorrow. A country with a high old-age dependency ratio is spending on pensions and healthcare today with no equivalent future payoff in workforce size.

body.caption: This slice is the one driving the 'pension time bomb' language used for Japan and much of Europe, covered later in this chapter.

body.title: Calculate a Dependency Ratio
body.prompt: A country has 10 lakh (10,00,000) people. Of these, 2.5 lakh are aged 0 to 14, 6.2 lakh are aged 15 to 64, and 1.3 lakh are aged 65 and above. What is the total dependency ratio, in percent, rounded to one decimal place?
body.explanation: Add the dependents: 2.5 lakh (0 to 14) plus 1.3 lakh (65 plus) equals 3.8 lakh. Divide by the working-age population of 6.2 lakh, which gives approximately 0.6129, then multiply by 100 to get 61.3%. In practical terms, every 100 working-age people in this country are supporting roughly 61 dependents, a relatively high burden that suggests a country still fairly early in its transition.

children.text: India's Dependency Ratio Trajectory: The Window Behind the Dividend

India's total dependency ratio has fallen sharply since independence, and that decline is the single mechanical driver behind the 'demographic dividend' phrase used so loosely in business news. Fewer dependents per working-age person means more of national income can flow into savings, investment, and consumption, rather than being absorbed by the basic needs of children and the elderly.

body.title: Quick Check: Reading the Shape
body.question: You are shown a population pyramid where the 65 plus age band is wider than the 0 to 14 age band, and the narrowest part of the entire chart is the base. What does this shape most likely indicate?
options: A young, rapidly growing population in Stage 2
A country with a very high youth dependency ratio
A contracting, sub-replacement population in Stage 5
A country with no meaningful dependency burden at all
body.explanation: A base narrower than the top, with more elderly than children, is the defining signature of a contracting or urn-shaped pyramid, seen in Stage 5 countries like Japan. The dependency burden here is dominated by the old-age ratio, not the youth ratio, and it tends to keep rising as the shrinking working-age band ages into retirement itself.

body.text: A falling dependency ratio is an opportunity, not a guarantee. South Korea and Japan both passed through India's current position decades ago, with strikingly different long-run outcomes depending on how much of that window was spent building jobs, skills, and savings infrastructure versus being left on the table. This course returns to exactly that risk in Chapter 3.

The dependency ratio is not a side statistic. It is the single number that best explains why a country's savings rate, tax base, and government budget priorities shift the way they do, years before any of it becomes a headline.

points: A population pyramid stacks 5-year age bands by sex, and its overall shape, expansive, constrictive, or contracting, maps directly onto the demographic transition stages from the previous lesson.
The dependency ratio converts a pyramid into one comparable number: dependents (aged under 15 and 65 plus) per 100 working-age people (aged 15 to 64).
Splitting the ratio into youth and old-age components matters, since a youth-heavy burden funds a future workforce while an old-age burden funds pensions with no equivalent future payoff.
India's total dependency ratio has fallen from roughly 79 in 1971 to around 48 today, and is projected to trough in the 2030s before old-age dependency pushes it back up.
A falling dependency ratio opens a window for a demographic dividend, it does not automatically deliver one, which is exactly the risk this course examines next in India's own case.
